title: The navigator that drifted
intro: An inertial navigation unit integrates accelerometer data to track position. Its reported position drifts steadily away from GPS — always in the same direction, always at the same rate. Open the clues.

facts.label: The symptom
facts.value: Reported position falls behind the true track by a constant amount per second. After an hour the gap is large; after two hours it is exactly twice as large.

facts.label: The accelerometer
facts.value: Bench-calibrated this month. Bias within spec, noise within spec. Integrating its output over a stationary period yields zero velocity, correctly.

facts.label: The arithmetic
facts.value: Velocity is obtained by integrating acceleration; position by integrating velocity. Both integrals verified against closed-form test signals and correct to machine precision.

facts.label: The start
facts.value: The unit was switched on while the vehicle was already moving at cruise, rolling off the end of a transit leg.

facts.label: The initialisation
facts.value: Velocity is seeded at zero at power-on. There is no field to supply a starting velocity, and nothing in the log records one.

facts.label: The shape
facts.value: The drift is linear in time, not growing or oscillating. A plot of reported-versus-true position is two parallel lines.

composition.label: The integration constant was assumed zero

question: What actually failed?
choices: Accelerometer bias is being integrated twice and accumulating
The integration constant — the initial velocity — was assumed to be zero while the vehicle was already moving, so every velocity since is off by that constant and position drifts linearly
The numerical integration scheme is accumulating round-off error
The GPS reference itself is offset
debrief:
The arithmetic is exact and the sensor is healthy. What was lost is **+ C** — and in this system + C has a name: the **initial velocity**.

Integrating acceleration gives velocity *up to a constant*. Seeding that constant at zero asserts the vehicle was stationary at power-on. It was not; it was already at cruise. Every velocity since is short by that fixed amount, and integrating a constant velocity error gives a position error that grows **linearly** with time — which is precisely the shape in the last clue. Two parallel lines is the signature of a missing constant, not of a noisy sensor.

The clue that rules out the usual suspect is the bench calibration: an accelerometer *bias* integrated twice produces error growing with t², a curve that accelerates away. This one does not bend. Nor can round-off produce a perfectly steady, single-direction offset.

The fix is not better integration. It is a measurement: seed the velocity from GPS, or from the known state at power-on. That is the lesson underneath the whole concept — the shape is recoverable from the data, the offset never is, and a default of zero is a claim about the world that someone has to be willing to defend.
